hook.text: A company follows every rule but still harms customers. Legal? Yes. Ethical? Not even close.

buildup.text: Compliance means following rules. Ethics means doing the right thing even when no rule requires it.

discovery.text: Wells Fargo's fake accounts came from employees following aggressive sales targets. Not illegal — at first.

twist.text: Companies that rely solely on compliance create cultures that game rules rather than serve customers.

climax.text: Ethics fills the gaps between rules. Where compliance ends, ethical judgment must begin.

punchline.text: Compliance follows the rules. Ethics does what's right.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between ethics and compliance?
options: Ethics means doing right even without a rule; compliance means following rules
They are exactly the same thing
Compliance is always more important than ethics

hook.text: Ethical companies outperform unethical ones by 7.1% annually. Doing good and doing well aren't opposites.

buildup.text: Research shows that companies with strong ethical cultures have higher employee retention and customer loyalty.

discovery.text: Ethisphere's World's Most Ethical Companies index has outperformed the S&P 500 every year since 2007.

twist.text: The business case is strong, but most companies still treat ethics as a cost center, not a competitive advantage.

climax.text: Ethics isn't just about avoiding fines. It drives trust, loyalty, and long-term profitability.

punchline.text: Ethical companies outperform. Doing good pays off.

quiz.question: How do the most ethical companies perform financially?
options: They outperform the S&P 500 index consistently
They always lose money to competitors
Ethics has no effect on financial performance

hook.text: A bank knows the government will bail it out if it fails. So it takes riskier bets. That's moral hazard.

buildup.text: Moral hazard occurs when someone takes more risk because they won't bear the full consequences of failure.

discovery.text: The 2008 bailouts created massive moral hazard: banks learned that being too big to fail meant too big to punish.

twist.text: Insurance creates moral hazard too. People with flood insurance build in flood zones they'd otherwise avoid.

climax.text: Moral hazard is everywhere in business. Reducing it requires aligning consequences with risk-taking.

punchline.text: No consequences for failure. More reckless risk-taking.

quiz.question: What is moral hazard?
options: Taking more risk because you won't bear the consequences
A type of financial insurance
A legal liability for ethical violations

hook.text: Milton Friedman said a company's only duty is profit. Ed Freeman said it owes duties to all stakeholders.

buildup.text: Shareholder theory maximizes owner returns. Stakeholder theory balances employees, communities, and the environment.

discovery.text: In 2019, the Business Roundtable redefined corporate purpose to include all stakeholders, not just shareholders.

twist.text: Critics call stakeholder theory vague. Who decides which stakeholder matters most when interests conflict?

climax.text: The debate isn't settled. But companies ignoring non-shareholder interests face mounting pressure and regulation.

punchline.text: Profit for shareholders? Or value for all? The debate rages.

quiz.question: What did the Business Roundtable redefine in 2019?
options: Corporate purpose to include all stakeholders, not just shareholders
The legal definition of a corporation
The minimum wage for executives

hook.text: Good people make bad choices. Not because they're evil, but because they don't see the ethical issue at all.

buildup.text: Ethical blind spots are psychological biases that prevent us from recognizing ethical dimensions of our decisions.

discovery.text: Max Bazerman's research shows that framing a decision as 'business' rather than 'ethical' changes behavior dramatically.

twist.text: People rate themselves as more ethical than average. This overconfidence stops them scrutinizing their own choices.

climax.text: Recognizing ethical blind spots is the first step. Training and diverse perspectives reveal what we can't see.

punchline.text: Good people. Bad choices. They never saw the ethical issue.

quiz.question: What are ethical blind spots?
options: Biases that prevent recognizing ethical dimensions of decisions
A type of vision impairment
Deliberately ignoring ethical rules

hook.text: The Hippocratic Oath dates to 400 BC. It was the first professional code of conduct: 'First, do no harm.'

buildup.text: Professional codes spread from medicine to law, engineering, and eventually corporate business.

discovery.text: After Enron's collapse in 2001, Sarbanes-Oxley required public companies to adopt and disclose codes of ethics.

twist.text: Enron had a 64-page code of ethics. The board suspended it twice to approve deals that eventually destroyed the company.

climax.text: Codes matter only if enforced. A code on paper that leadership ignores is worse than having no code at all.

punchline.text: Enron had a 64-page code. They suspended it. Twice.

quiz.question: What happened with Enron's code of ethics?
options: The board suspended it twice to approve risky deals
It was the gold standard for corporate ethics
The company never had one

hook.text: Most employees can't name a single rule from their company's code of conduct. That's a problem.

buildup.text: Effective codes are clear, specific, and illustrated with real scenarios rather than abstract principles.

discovery.text: Google's original 'Don't Be Evil' code was memorable precisely because it was simple and direct.

twist.text: Codes that are too long become shelfware. Codes that are too short lack useful guidance for real decisions.

climax.text: The best codes provide principles plus examples. They answer 'what should I do when?' not just 'what's the rule?'

punchline.text: Clear. Specific. Memorable. That's an effective code.

quiz.question: What makes a code of conduct effective?
options: Clear principles with real scenarios and examples
Being as long and detailed as possible
Using complex legal language

hook.text: An auditor owns stock in the company she audits. Can she be objective? Every code of conduct says no.

buildup.text: Conflicts of interest occur when personal interests could influence professional judgment or decisions.

discovery.text: Arthur Andersen audited Enron while also earning $25 million in consulting fees from them. Objectivity was impossible.

twist.text: Research shows people can't be objective even when they try. Disclosure alone doesn't eliminate the bias.

climax.text: Managing conflicts requires avoidance or separation, not just disclosure. Knowing about a conflict doesn't fix it.

punchline.text: You audit them. You consult for them. You can't be objective.

quiz.question: Why is disclosure alone insufficient for conflicts of interest?
options: People can't be truly objective even when they try
Disclosure is illegal in most countries
Conflicts of interest don't actually exist

hook.text: A vendor sends your team Super Bowl tickets worth $5,000. Is it a gift or a bribe? The answer depends on your policy.

buildup.text: Gift policies set thresholds for acceptable gifts and entertainment to prevent improper influence on decisions.

discovery.text: The FCPA and UK Bribery Act treat excessive gifts to government officials as bribery, even if culturally normal.

twist.text: In many countries, refusing a gift is deeply offensive. But accepting it may violate anti-corruption laws.

climax.text: Gift policies navigate the line between relationship-building and corruption. Clear rules protect everyone involved.

punchline.text: Super Bowl tickets. A gift? Or a bribe? Policy decides.

quiz.question: Why do companies have gift and entertainment policies?
options: To prevent improper influence on business decisions
To save money on corporate spending
To punish generous employees

hook.text: An employee tweets about an unannounced product launch. The stock price moves. The SEC investigates.

buildup.text: Social media blurs the line between personal expression and corporate communication. Codes must address both.

discovery.text: In 2013, the SEC confirmed that social media posts can count as material disclosures under securities law.

twist.text: Employees often don't realize their personal posts can create legal liability for their employer.

climax.text: Modern codes of conduct must address social media explicitly. The boundaries need to be clear before an incident occurs.

punchline.text: Personal tweet. Stock moves. SEC investigates. Know the rules.

quiz.question: How do social media posts relate to securities law?
options: Posts can count as material disclosures under SEC rules
Social media is entirely outside regulatory scope
Only CEO posts are regulated

hook.text: Sherron Watkins warned Enron's CEO about accounting fraud. He ignored her. She went public. Enron collapsed.

buildup.text: Whistleblowers expose wrongdoing that organizations try to hide — from fraud to safety violations to corruption.

discovery.text: Cynthia Cooper uncovered WorldCom's $3.8 billion fraud. Time named her Person of the Year in 2002.

twist.text: Most whistleblowers face retaliation. Studies show 82% experience harassment, demotion, or termination.

climax.text: Whistleblowers protect the public at great personal cost. They deserve protection, not punishment.

punchline.text: She warned them. They ignored her. She saved us all.

quiz.question: What did Cynthia Cooper uncover?
options: WorldCom's $3.8 billion accounting fraud
Enron's energy trading manipulation
Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme

hook.text: You report fraud at your company and get fired the next week. Is that legal? It depends on where you live.

buildup.text: Whistleblower protection laws shield reporters from retaliation — firing, demotion, and harassment.

discovery.text: The US Dodd-Frank Act lets whistleblowers earn 10-30% of SEC penalties exceeding $1 million.

twist.text: Despite legal protections, enforcement is slow and uncertain. Many whistleblowers still face years of litigation.

climax.text: Legal protections are necessary but insufficient. Cultural change is needed to make whistleblowing safe.

punchline.text: Laws protect whistleblowers. But retaliation still happens.

quiz.question: What reward does the Dodd-Frank Act offer whistleblowers?
options: 10-30% of SEC penalties exceeding $1 million
A guaranteed new job
Full immunity from all prosecution

hook.text: Your company has a hotline for reporting misconduct. You call. Nothing happens. Do you try again or go to the SEC?

buildup.text: Internal reporting channels — hotlines, ethics portals, ombudspersons — let employees raise concerns internally first.

discovery.text: ACFE data shows that tips are the number one way fraud is detected, catching 43% of all cases.

twist.text: But 50% of employees who witness misconduct don't report it. Fear and distrust in the process are the top reasons.

climax.text: Effective reporting channels require anonymity, responsiveness, and visible follow-through to build trust.

punchline.text: Tips catch 43% of fraud. But half who see it stay silent.

quiz.question: What percentage of fraud is detected through tips?

hook.text: A compliance officer reports accounting irregularities. She's moved to a windowless office. Her projects disappear.

buildup.text: Retaliation against whistleblowers takes many forms: termination, isolation, reassignment, and career sabotage.

discovery.text: Retaliation doesn't just hurt the individual. It sends a message to every other employee: stay silent or suffer.

twist.text: Companies that retaliate against whistleblowers face larger fines. Courts treat retaliation as evidence of guilt.

climax.text: Retaliation is the most effective way to destroy an ethics program. It proves the code of conduct is meaningless.

punchline.text: Punish the reporter. Silence everyone else. Guarantee more fraud.

quiz.question: How do courts view retaliation against whistleblowers?
options: As evidence of guilt that increases fines
As a normal business practice
As irrelevant to the original complaint

hook.text: Since 2011, the SEC has awarded over $1.5 billion to whistleblowers. The largest single award exceeded $279 million.

buildup.text: The SEC's whistleblower program pays individuals who report securities violations leading to successful enforcement.

discovery.text: The program received over 18,000 tips in 2023 alone. It has fundamentally changed how fraud is detected.

twist.text: Financial incentives create a tension: are whistleblowers motivated by justice or money? The SEC says it doesn't matter.

climax.text: The program works. It deters fraud, accelerates detection, and gives companies a reason to catch problems first.

punchline.text: $1.5 billion awarded. 18,000 tips yearly. The program works.

quiz.question: How much has the SEC awarded to whistleblowers since 2011?
options: Over $1.5 billion
About $10 million
They don't pay whistleblowers

hook.text: The DOJ evaluates compliance programs on three questions: well designed, applied in good faith, and does it work?

buildup.text: The US Sentencing Guidelines define seven elements of an effective compliance program, from leadership to monitoring.

discovery.text: Key elements include risk assessment, policies, training, reporting systems, enforcement, and continuous improvement.

twist.text: Having all elements on paper isn't enough. The DOJ specifically asks whether the program actually works in practice.

climax.text: A compliance program is a living system. It must adapt to new risks, learn from incidents, and prove its effectiveness.

punchline.text: Well designed. Applied earnestly. Does it actually work?

quiz.question: What three questions does the DOJ ask about compliance programs?
options: Well designed, applied in good faith, and does it work?
Is it written, signed, and filed?
Is it cheap, fast, and automated?

hook.text: The CEO says ethics matter in every speech. Then she promotes the top seller who breaks every rule. Actions win.

buildup.text: Tone at the top means leadership demonstrates ethical behavior through actions, not just words.

discovery.text: Research shows that employees take ethical cues from leaders. If leaders cut corners, the whole organization follows.

twist.text: Middle management is actually more influential than the CEO. They translate executive ethics into daily behavior.

climax.text: Ethical culture flows from leadership to the front line. Every management layer either reinforces or undermines it.

punchline.text: The CEO talks ethics. Then promotes the rule-breaker. Actions win.

quiz.question: Why is 'tone at the top' important?
options: Employees take ethical cues from leadership behavior
It's required by law to give ethics speeches
It only affects the executive suite

hook.text: Annual compliance training: click through slides, pass the quiz, forget everything. Sound familiar?

buildup.text: Traditional compliance training focuses on rules and policies. Effective training focuses on judgment and dilemmas.

discovery.text: Scenario-based training that presents ethical dilemmas improves decision-making 3x more than slide-based training.

twist.text: The best training doesn't teach answers. It teaches employees how to recognize and reason through ethical issues.

climax.text: Ethics training should build moral muscle, not check a compliance box. Real scenarios, real discussions, real impact.

punchline.text: Click, pass, forget. That's not training. That's a checkbox.

quiz.question: What makes ethics training most effective?
options: Scenario-based dilemmas that build judgment skills
Longer slide presentations with more content
Automated quizzes with instant feedback

hook.text: A compliance program untested is a compliance program unknown. You don't know if it works until you check.

buildup.text: Monitoring is continuous observation of controls. Testing is periodic deep-dive assessment of whether they work.

discovery.text: The DOJ considers whether companies proactively test their programs, not just respond to problems after they occur.

twist.text: Many companies monitor what's easy to measure, not what matters. Counting training completions doesn't measure culture.

climax.text: Effective monitoring combines quantitative metrics with qualitative culture assessments for a complete picture.

punchline.text: Untested controls. Unknown effectiveness. That's not compliance.

quiz.question: What's the difference between monitoring and testing?
options: Monitoring is continuous observation; testing is periodic deep assessment
They are the same thing
Monitoring is for IT; testing is for legal

hook.text: Your supplier uses child labor. You didn't know. Regulators say you should have. The fine is $50 million.

buildup.text: Companies are responsible for the ethical conduct of their vendors, partners, and agents under many regulations.

discovery.text: The FCPA holds companies liable for bribery committed by third-party agents, even without direct knowledge.

twist.text: Most compliance failures involving third parties happen because due diligence was skipped to close deals faster.

climax.text: Third-party risk management requires screening before engagement and monitoring throughout the relationship.

punchline.text: Your supplier broke the law. You didn't check. You pay.

quiz.question: Why is third-party due diligence important?
options: Companies can be held liable for their partners' ethical violations
It's only needed for government contracts
Third parties are never a compliance risk

hook.text: Elizabeth Holmes promised to revolutionize blood testing. The technology never worked. She raised $700 million anyway.

buildup.text: Theranos claimed to run hundreds of tests from a single drop of blood. Investors and partners believed the vision.

discovery.text: Whistleblowers revealed that Theranos secretly used conventional machines while claiming its technology worked.

twist.text: Board members included Henry Kissinger and James Mattis — impressive names but no medical or tech expertise.

climax.text: Holmes was convicted of fraud in 2022. Theranos is now a case study in what happens when culture punishes doubt.

punchline.text: The tech never worked. She raised $700 million. Nobody asked.

quiz.question: What did whistleblowers reveal about Theranos?
options: It secretly used conventional machines while claiming new technology worked
Its technology was better than advertised
It was making too much profit

hook.text: Volkswagen's cars passed emissions tests perfectly. On the road, they emitted 40 times the legal limit of pollutants.

buildup.text: VW installed 'defeat devices' — software that detected when a car was being tested and reduced emissions temporarily.

discovery.text: Researchers at West Virginia University discovered the discrepancy in 2014 using real-world road testing.

twist.text: The fraud wasn't one person's idea. Engineers, managers, and executives all participated over nearly a decade.

climax.text: VW paid over $30 billion in fines and settlements. Several executives went to prison. Culture enabled the fraud.

punchline.text: Passed every test. Failed on every road. Software cheated.

quiz.question: How did VW cheat on emissions tests?
options: Software detected testing and temporarily reduced emissions
They modified the testing equipment
They bribed the testing agencies

hook.text: Two 737 MAX planes crashed in five months. 346 people died. Internal emails showed employees knew about the risks.

buildup.text: Boeing's MCAS system could push the nose down based on a single sensor reading. Pilots weren't told it existed.

discovery.text: An internal review found Boeing employees mocking regulators and boasting about minimizing pilot training requirements.

twist.text: Boeing had shifted from an engineering-first culture to a cost-cutting culture. Safety became a budget line item.

climax.text: The MAX crisis shows how cultural erosion kills. When profit consistently overrides safety, disaster is inevitable.

punchline.text: 346 lives. Employees knew the risks. Cost-cutting won.

quiz.question: What cultural shift contributed to the 737 MAX crashes?
options: Boeing moved from engineering-first to cost-cutting culture
Boeing hired too many engineers
Pilots received too much training

topics.title: The Opioid Crisis and Pharma Ethics

hook.text: Purdue Pharma told doctors OxyContin wasn't addictive. Over 500,000 Americans died from opioid overdoses.

buildup.text: Purdue aggressively marketed OxyContin while minimizing addiction risks. Sales reps were rewarded for volume.

discovery.text: Internal documents showed Purdue knew about high addiction rates but continued marketing the drug as safe.

twist.text: The Sackler family extracted $10 billion from Purdue before declaring bankruptcy to limit liability.

climax.text: The opioid crisis is the deadliest corporate ethical failure. Profits were chosen over hundreds of thousands of lives.

punchline.text: Not addictive, they said. 500,000 dead. They knew.

quiz.question: What did Purdue Pharma's internal documents show?
options: They knew about high addiction rates but marketed OxyContin as safe
OxyContin was never actually sold in the US
The drug was less effective than advertised

hook.text: Wells Fargo employees created 3.5 million fake accounts to meet sales targets. Management called it 'cross-selling.'

buildup.text: The bank's 'Eight is Great' campaign pushed employees to open eight products per customer, regardless of need.

discovery.text: Employees who refused to create fake accounts were fired. Those who called ethics hotlines faced retaliation.

twist.text: CEO John Stumpf initially blamed 5,300 low-level employees. He was eventually forced to resign and return $41 million.

climax.text: Toxic incentives created the fraud. A culture of fear sustained it. The failure was systemic, not individual.

punchline.text: 3.5 million fake accounts. Blame the tellers. Culture did this.

quiz.question: What drove Wells Fargo employees to create fake accounts?
options: Aggressive sales targets and fear of being fired
A computer system error
Customer requests for multiple accounts

hook.text: Can you measure culture? Yes. Anonymous surveys, hotline trends, exit interviews, and audit findings all tell a story.

buildup.text: Culture measurement combines quantitative data — report rates, resolution times — with qualitative employee feedback.

discovery.text: The Ethics & Compliance Initiative found that only 21% of employees believe their company has a strong ethical culture.

twist.text: Companies that measure culture regularly detect problems earlier. Those that don't are surprised by scandals.

climax.text: You manage what you measure. If you don't measure culture, you can't improve it.

punchline.text: Only 21% see strong culture. Measure it to improve it.

quiz.question: What percentage of employees believe their company has a strong ethical culture?

hook.text: An employee spots a compliance risk but stays quiet. Why? She saw what happened to the last person who spoke up.

buildup.text: Psychological safety means employees can raise concerns without fear of punishment, embarrassment, or retaliation.

discovery.text: Google's Project Aristotle found that psychological safety was the single most important factor in team effectiveness.

twist.text: Compliance programs depend on people speaking up. Without psychological safety, reporting channels are useless.

climax.text: Building psychological safety requires leaders to model vulnerability, reward reporting, and respond constructively.

punchline.text: Speak up safely. Or stay silent. Culture decides which.

quiz.question: What did Google's Project Aristotle find?
options: Psychological safety is the most important factor in team effectiveness
Technical skills matter most
Team size determines success

hook.text: Show me your incentives and I'll show you your outcomes. Every scandal traces back to misaligned rewards.

buildup.text: People respond to incentives. Reward sales volume, you get aggressive selling. Reward ethics, you get ethical behavior.

discovery.text: After its scandal, Wells Fargo eliminated sales targets and tied bonuses to customer satisfaction instead.

twist.text: Ethical incentives are harder to measure than financial ones. Most companies default to what's easy to count.

climax.text: Aligning incentives with ethics is the most powerful lever for culture change. Everything else is window dressing.

punchline.text: Reward ethics. Get ethics. Reward sales. Get scandals.

quiz.question: What change did Wells Fargo make after its scandal?
options: Eliminated sales targets and tied bonuses to customer satisfaction
Increased sales targets to recover losses
Replaced all employees

hook.text: Before every major decision, ask: is it legal, is it ethical, and would I be comfortable seeing it on the news?

buildup.text: Ethical decision frameworks provide structured tests that employees can apply to real business situations.

discovery.text: Johnson & Johnson's credo guided their 1982 Tylenol recall. They prioritized safety over profit and won lasting trust.

twist.text: Frameworks fail if they're only consulted during crises. Ethics must be embedded in routine processes and reviews.

climax.text: Ethical decisions are habits, not heroic acts. Build ethics into daily processes and it becomes automatic.

punchline.text: Legal? Ethical? Front page test? Ask before you decide.

quiz.question: How did J&J's credo guide the 1982 Tylenol crisis?
options: They prioritized customer safety over profit in the recall decision
They delayed the recall to protect stock price
They blamed the retailer for the contamination

hook.text: AI can monitor every employee communication for misconduct. But should it? Ethics meets technology at the frontier.

buildup.text: RegTech uses AI to automate compliance monitoring, flag risks, and analyze patterns humans can't detect.

discovery.text: AI ethics tools can detect bias in hiring, lending, and insurance decisions before they cause harm.

twist.text: Surveillance-based compliance undermines trust. If employees feel watched, they comply out of fear, not conviction.

climax.text: The future of compliance culture balances technology's power with human judgment and respect for privacy.

punchline.text: AI monitors everything. Trust evaporates. Balance is key.

quiz.question: What is the main tension in AI-powered compliance?
options: Surveillance capabilities versus employee trust and privacy
AI is too expensive for most companies
AI cannot detect any compliance issues
